description: Gold Q&A set for the card-generation quality check (rubric item 7f). Known-correct MCAT organic-chemistry mechanism facts. Generated cards are checked against these answers + acceptable_variants by mechgrader.cardgen.check.
source_ref_note: The source_ref values below are ILLUSTRATIVE placeholders naming a textbook + chapter/section. They are NOT yet entries in sources/registry.json (which ships only the non-resolvable EXAMPLE-textbook). Before this gold set gates any real generated card, each source_id must be registered in sources/registry.json AND its exact locator verified against the physical source. See data/gold_qa/README.md.

item_format.question: the prompt
item_format.notes: what makes a generated card useful vs bad-teaching here

items.question: In an SN2 reaction, what happens to the stereochemistry at the electrophilic carbon?
items.notes: Useful cards tie inversion to backside attack; 'the stereochemistry changes' is too vague.

items.question: What is the overall rate order (molecularity) of the SN2 reaction?
items.notes: SN2 is second order overall; a card claiming first order is wrong.

items.question: Which substrate class reacts fastest in an SN2 reaction?
items.notes: Steric access controls SN2; tertiary is essentially unreactive by SN2.

items.question: How does increasing steric bulk at the reacting carbon affect the SN2 rate?
items.notes: Backside attack is blocked by bulk; a card saying it increases the rate is wrong.

items.question: How many elementary steps does the SN2 mechanism have?
items.notes: Bond making and breaking are simultaneous; contrast with the two-step SN1.

items.question: What is the rate-determining step of an SN1 reaction?
acceptable_variants: loss of the leaving group to form a carbocation
items.notes: The slow step is ionization; the nucleophile does not appear in the rate law.

items.question: What is the rate order of the SN1 reaction?
items.notes: Rate depends only on the substrate; a card saying it depends on nucleophile concentration is wrong.

items.question: Which substrate class reacts fastest in an SN1 reaction?
items.notes: Carbocation stability drives SN1; a card saying primary is wrong.

items.question: What is the stereochemical outcome at a stereocenter formed in an SN1 reaction?
items.notes: The planar carbocation is attacked from both faces; useful cards mention the planar intermediate.

items.question: What is the key reactive intermediate in an SN1 reaction?
items.notes: Its stability explains SN1 substrate and rearrangement behavior.

items.question: What is the rate-determining step of an E1 reaction?
acceptable_variants: loss of the leaving group to form a carbocation
items.notes: E1 shares its slow ionization step (and intermediate) with SN1.

items.question: Which alkene is the major (Zaitsev) product of a typical E1 or E2 elimination?
items.notes: Zaitsev = more substituted/more stable; contrast with the Hofmann (less substituted) product.

items.question: What is the rate order of the E1 reaction?
items.notes: Like SN1, the base/nucleophile does not appear in the E1 rate law.

items.question: What geometric relationship between the leaving group and the beta-hydrogen must the E2 transition state achieve?
items.notes: The C-H and C-LG bonds must be anti-periplanar; a card saying syn-periplanar is wrong for the typical case.

items.question: What is the rate order of the E2 reaction?
items.notes: Both substrate and base appear in the rate law.

items.question: How many elementary steps does the E2 mechanism have?
items.notes: Deprotonation and leaving-group loss are simultaneous.

items.question: What kind of base favors E2 over SN2 for a given substrate?
acceptable_variants: a bulky base such as tert-butoxide
items.notes: Bulk disfavors backside substitution and favors deprotonation.

items.question: Using a bulky base pushes an elimination toward which regiochemical product?
items.notes: Steric approach control gives the less-substituted alkene; useful cards name the bulky base.

items.question: What regiochemistry does addition of HBr to an alkene follow in the absence of peroxides?
acceptable_variants: H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens
items.notes: Proton adds to give the more stable carbocation; contrast with radical anti-Markovnikov.

items.question: What reactive intermediate forms during electrophilic addition of HX to an alkene?
items.notes: Its stability sets Markovnikov regiochemistry and possible rearrangements.

items.question: What regiochemistry results from radical addition of HBr to an alkene (with peroxides)?
acceptable_variants: Br adds to the less substituted carbon
items.notes: Only HBr does this radical chain; a card claiming Markovnikov here is wrong.

items.question: What is the stereochemistry of Br2 (bromine) addition across an alkene?
items.notes: The bromonium ion forces backside opening; a card saying syn addition is wrong.

items.question: What cyclic intermediate forms when Br2 adds to an alkene?
items.notes: The three-membered bromonium ion explains anti stereochemistry.

items.question: What regiochemistry does oxymercuration-demercuration give, and does it rearrange?
items.notes: The mercurinium ion prevents rearrangement while keeping Markovnikov selectivity.

items.question: What regiochemistry does hydroboration-oxidation give?
acceptable_variants: OH adds to the less substituted carbon
items.notes: Boron adds to the less hindered carbon (syn); useful cards note the syn addition too.

items.question: What is the first step of electrophilic aromatic substitution?
items.answer: the arene attacks the electrophile to form an arenium ion (sigma complex)
acceptable_variants: attack of the ring on the electrophile
items.notes: The rate-determining step forms the resonance-stabilized arenium ion.

items.question: Are -OH, -NH2, and alkyl groups ortho/para directors or meta directors in EAS?
items.notes: These activators are ortho/para directing; contrast with deactivating meta directors.

items.question: Is a nitro (-NO2) group an activating ortho/para director or a deactivating meta director?
items.notes: Strong electron withdrawal deactivates and directs meta.

items.question: What step restores aromaticity at the end of electrophilic aromatic substitution?
items.notes: Rearomatization by proton loss, not by adding a nucleophile (that would be addition, not substitution).

items.question: What type of catalyst is required for Friedel-Crafts acylation?
items.notes: The Lewis acid generates the acylium electrophile.

items.question: At approximately what angle does a nucleophile attack a carbonyl (the Buergi-Dunitz trajectory)?
items.notes: Nucleophile approaches the carbonyl carbon slightly off the C=O axis.

items.question: What product results when a ketone is reduced by NaBH4 or LiAlH4?
items.notes: Hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon; a ketone gives a secondary alcohol.

items.question: What product results when an aldehyde is reduced by a hydride reagent?
items.notes: Aldehydes give primary alcohols; ketones give secondary alcohols.

items.question: Which atom of a carbonyl group does a nucleophile attack?
items.notes: The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic; the oxygen is nucleophilic/basic.

items.question: In carbonyl chemistry, does a Grignard reagent act as a nucleophile or an electrophile?
items.notes: The polarized C-Mg bond makes carbon nucleophilic (and strongly basic).

items.question: What high-energy intermediate is common to nucleophilic acyl substitution reactions?
items.notes: Addition then elimination proceeds through the tetrahedral intermediate.

items.question: Which carboxylic acid derivative is the most reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
items.notes: Best leaving group and least resonance donation into the carbonyl.

items.question: Which carboxylic acid derivative is the least reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
items.notes: Strong nitrogen resonance donation stabilizes the carbonyl and worsens the leaving group.

items.question: What structural factor best explains the reactivity order of carboxylic acid derivatives?
acceptable_variants: how good the leaving group is
items.notes: Better leaving group = more reactive derivative (acyl chloride > anhydride > ester > amide).

items.question: What nucleophile adds to the electrophilic carbonyl in an aldol addition?
items.notes: The base-generated enolate is the nucleophilic carbon.

items.question: What product forms after an aldol condensation undergoes dehydration?
items.notes: Loss of water gives the conjugated enone; the plain aldol (before dehydration) is a beta-hydroxy carbonyl.

items.question: Why is the alpha-carbon of a carbonyl acidic?
acceptable_variants: the conjugate base (enolate) is stabilized by resonance
items.notes: Deprotonation gives a resonance-delocalized enolate; useful cards mention delocalization onto oxygen.

items.question: What catalyst is used in a Fischer esterification?
items.notes: Acid activates the carbonyl and the leaving group; Fischer esterification is acid-catalyzed.

items.question: How is the equilibrium of a Fischer esterification driven toward the ester?
items.answer: by Le Chatelier (excess alcohol or removing water)
acceptable_variants: remove water or add excess alcohol
items.notes: It is a reversible equilibrium, so it is driven by removing product or adding reactant.

items.question: In acid-catalyzed ester hydrolysis, what species acts as the nucleophile?
items.notes: Water attacks the protonated carbonyl; distinguish from base hydrolysis (hydroxide).

items.question: Which tautomer is generally more stable for a simple aldehyde or ketone?
items.notes: The C=O keto form is usually favored over the enol; a card saying the enol is more stable is wrong for simple carbonyls.

items.question: Keto-enol tautomerization is catalyzed by what?
items.notes: Both pathways exist; useful cards sketch the enol via acid and the enolate via base.

items.question: In an acid-base proton transfer, which side does the equilibrium favor?
items.answer: the side with the weaker acid and weaker base
acceptable_variants: formation of the weaker acid and base
items.notes: Equilibrium favors the more stable (weaker) conjugate acid/base.

items.question: A lower pKa corresponds to what kind of acid?
items.notes: Lower pKa = stronger acid; a card saying lower pKa means weaker acid is wrong.

items.question: Which reagent oxidizes a primary alcohol to an aldehyde and stops there?
items.notes: PCC is anhydrous/mild and stops at the aldehyde; Jones/KMnO4 would over-oxidize.

items.question: To what product does Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4) oxidize a primary alcohol?
items.notes: Aqueous strong Cr(VI) over-oxidizes past the aldehyde to the acid.

items.question: What product forms when a secondary alcohol is oxidized?
items.notes: Secondary alcohols give ketones (no further oxidation without C-C cleavage).

items.question: Which carbonyl types does NaBH4 selectively reduce?
acceptable_variants: aldehydes/ketones but not esters or acids
items.notes: NaBH4 is mild: it does not reduce esters or carboxylic acids well; contrast with LiAlH4.

items.question: Which functional groups can the strong reductant LiAlH4 reduce that NaBH4 generally cannot?
items.notes: LiAlH4 is a powerful hydride source; useful cards contrast it with milder NaBH4.

items.question: What is the stereochemistry of catalytic hydrogenation (H2/Pd) across an alkene?
items.notes: Both hydrogens add to the same face on the metal surface; a card saying anti is wrong.

items.question: What are the three phases of a radical chain mechanism, in order?
items.notes: A useful card can ask which step consumes/creates radicals net.

items.question: In radical halogenation, is bromination or chlorination more selective?
items.notes: The endothermic, late transition state of bromination makes it more selective (Hammond).

items.question: Which carbon radical is the most stable?
items.notes: Radical stability parallels carbocations: tertiary > secondary > primary.

items.question: What functional group forms when a primary amine reacts with an aldehyde or ketone?
items.notes: Primary amine -> imine; a card saying enamine is wrong (that needs a secondary amine).

items.question: What functional group forms when a secondary amine reacts with an aldehyde or ketone?
items.notes: Secondary amine -> enamine (no N-H left to lose, so the double bond goes to carbon).

items.question: Around what pH is imine formation typically fastest?
items.notes: Acid catalyzes dehydration but too much acid protonates the amine; the optimum is mildly acidic.

items.question: What product forms when an aldehyde reacts with two equivalents of alcohol under acid?
items.notes: One equivalent gives a hemiacetal; two give the acetal (with loss of water).

items.question: What common synthetic role do acetals serve?
items.answer: protecting groups for aldehydes and ketones
items.notes: Acetals are stable to base/nucleophiles and removed by aqueous acid.

items.question: How do sugars form a cyclic hemiacetal?
items.answer: an intramolecular hydroxyl adds to the carbonyl
acceptable_variants: intramolecular addition of an OH to the carbonyl
a hydroxyl in the same molecule attacks the carbonyl
items.notes: Ring closure of the open-chain sugar; the new stereocenter is the anomeric carbon.

items.question: What type of bond links two amino acids in a peptide?
items.notes: A peptide bond is an amide between the carboxyl of one residue and the amine of the next.

items.question: What class of enzymes catalyzes hydrolysis of peptide bonds?
items.notes: Proteases lower the huge kinetic barrier of amide hydrolysis.

items.question: What is the geometry of the peptide (amide) bond, and why?
items.answer: planar due to resonance (partial double-bond character)
items.notes: Nitrogen lone-pair delocalization gives partial C-N double-bond character and restricted rotation.

items.question: In phosphoryl transfer reactions, what role does ATP most often play?
items.notes: ATP donates a phosphoryl group to an acceptor (e.g., an enzyme or substrate hydroxyl).

items.question: What class of enzymes transfers a phosphoryl group from ATP to a substrate?
items.notes: Kinases catalyze phosphoryl transfer; phosphatases do the reverse hydrolysis.

items.question: Which metal ion is the usual cofactor that stabilizes ATP's phosphates during phosphoryl transfer?
items.notes: Mg2+ coordinates the phosphate oxygens and shields negative charge.

items.question: What catalytic triad do serine proteases use?
items.notes: The triad performs general base/covalent catalysis via a covalent acyl-enzyme intermediate.

items.question: How do enzymes increase reaction rates thermodynamically?
items.notes: Enzymes lower Ea (stabilize the transition state) without changing the overall equilibrium.

items.question: In covalent catalysis, what does the enzyme transiently form with the substrate?
acceptable_variants: a transient covalent bond to the substrate
items.notes: A transient covalent bond provides an alternative lower-energy path.
